column4: The command to fear the Lord is grounded in the tremendous convulsion of the Hour; this supplies the creation-wide terror by which the section says Ghashiya covers its subjects.
The quake makes nursing mothers forget, pregnancies end, and people look intoxicated although they are not; an outer event has penetrated awareness and bodily control.
Fire scorches their faces until their mouths contort, giving another direct staging of punishment reaching the exposed front of the person.
God makes earth a bed and sky a structure, then sends rain and brings out fruit; an overhead cover, the ground below, and productive growth form a life-giving enclosure.
The wrongdoers are surrounded by a fire whose enclosing walls are described like a pavilion; the architectural form of shelter becomes the material of punishment.
The believers inhabit gardens, wear garments, and recline on couches, supplying the sheltering counterpart to the fire-pavilion that encloses the wrongdoers in 18:29.
The deniers demand that pieces of sky be dropped on them; their challenge supplies the overhead fall answered by the punitive canopy in 26:189.
Sincere spending is like a high garden whose yield doubles under rain; this is the fruitful cultivated cover set against the fire-struck garden in the following ayah.
The rejecters' spending is likened to an icy wind that strikes and destroys a people's crop; their moral covering yields a visibly ruined planting.
The faithful prayer asks for good in both lives and protection from the punishment of Fire, repeating the section's protective stance in a compact supplication.
Those reflecting on creation ask their Lord to protect them from the punishment of Fire; cosmic perception culminates in the same request for a true shield.
The God-fearing are in gardens and bliss immediately before their protection from Hell is named, making the positive cover the setting of their rescue.
The Garden people rejoice because their Lord protected them from the punishment of the Blaze; it is a second direct formulation of the protective claim later voiced in 52:27.
The Garden people taste no further death and God protects them from the punishment of Hell; hidden reward and deliverance from the crushing cover coincide.
After their deeds rust over their hearts, they are veiled from their Lord on that Day; the inward cover of 83:14 reaches its final relational consequence.
God makes the sky a protected roof, yet people turn from its signs; the normal overhead expanse is a preserved shelter rather than the descending punitive cover.
God restrains the sky from falling upon earth except by His permission; the verse identifies divine mercy in holding the overhead cover safely in place.
A wall with a gate separates mercy on its inner side from punishment outside; one structure becomes the exact boundary between protective enclosure and punitive exposure.
Even if the deniers saw a piece of sky falling, they would call it a massed cloud; what appears capable of shade conceals the punishment they refuse to recognize.
God did not institute the protected livestock called hām, but disbelievers fabricated the rule; the related h-m-y protection term exposes a human-made sanctuary joined to kufr.
Faces are turned about in the Fire while their owners regret disobedience; the exposed front of the person remains the visible site on which punishment works.
When the promised punishment draws near, the faces of those who kafarū become distressed; the truth-coverer's face registers the arrival of what had been denied.
After the garden owner proves unable to protect himself, the passage says all protective authority belongs to God; this identifies the source of the only cover that endures.
The chastened garden owners hope their Lord will replace the lost plot with a better one; ruined cover becomes an occasion to seek a newly bestowed garden.
Neither wealth nor children avail those who kafarū against God, and they belong to the Fire; this identifies the people whose cultivated wealth is destroyed in the next ayah's comparison.
Their hearts are sealed because of covenant-breaking and kufr, so belief scarcely enters; covering truth is again answered by a closed faculty.
Those who prefer the nearer life over the Hereafter are identified as disbelievers whom God does not guide, establishing the choice behind the sealing described next.
God seals their hearts, hearing, and sight, leaving them heedless; the prior preference and kufr become a cover over every receiving faculty.
God extends the shadow and appoints the sun as its guide; the relation between overhead light and sheltering cover is presented as a deliberately governed sign.
God gradually draws the shadow back, making protective cover visibly removable rather than self-sustaining.
The Garden is brought near to the God-fearing after having been an unseen promise; what was covered from present perception becomes immediate.
The promised Garden belongs to one who feared the Merciful in the unseen and came with a returning heart; hidden reward answers hidden fear.
The warning asks whether people await God's decisive coming amid canopies of cloud; an overhead covering accompanies the arrival of settled judgment.
Shackles reach the rejecters' chins and constrain their heads immediately before barriers and covered sight are described; bodily enclosure precedes perceptual enclosure.
The two promised gardens possess spreading branches, giving a concise visual form to the tree-grown cover heard in the name jannah.
Those who disbelieve are asked to consider earth below and sky above, either of which could become punishment; their apparently stable enclosure depends wholly on God.
The arrival of the greatest overwhelming calamity supplies a close nonlexical name for the all-surpassing event that Ghashiya makes perceptible as a cover.
The verb تغشاها euphemistically describes one spouse covering the other before pregnancy begins; this may illuminate a life-producing bodily use of the root beside Ghashiya's destructive cover.
